The Ford Explorer's Latest NHTSA Investigation Covers 1.2 Million Vehicles
31 photos
Photo: Ford
The Explorer, which is Ford's best-selling sport utility vehicle in the Dearborn-based manufacturer's home market, has landed in another federal investigation. This time, the Office of Defects Investigation has learned that the seat-mounted side airbags may inflict serious burn injuries upon deployment.
PE26008 is what the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration calls this investigation, which covers a mammoth vehicle population. More specifically, an estimated 1,236,155 examples that FoMoCo produced at its Chicago assembly plant in the state of Illinois for model years 2021 through 2026.
The allegations concern drivers and front passengers who sustained burns during crashes that involved side-airbag deployment. Per the ODI, the injuries typically involved second- or third-degree burns. Complaints also identify law enforcement officers driving Explorer -based Police Interceptor Utility models.
So far, the federal watchdog has received 8 vehicle owner questionnaires and 4 Early Warning Reporting Death and Injury reports. A table provided by the NHTSA counts 11 incidents after removing duplicate submissions, with 10 involving burn injuries. Thankfully for everyone, the agency lists no fatalities.
Unlike side-curtain airbags, those mounted inside the front seats deploy alongside the occupant's torso during specific crashes. These airbags are designed to reduce the risk of injury in scenarios that include side impacts. The NHTSA's preliminary evaluation document fails to explain why the reported side-airbag deployments allegedly produced second- and third-degree burns.
Photo: Ford As things stand now, it would be foolish to put the blame on the inflator, the airbag's fabric, deployment pressure, hot gases, or the position of the occupant relative to the airbag. The agency needs time and more data, hopefully from the Ford Motor Company and the airbag supplier as well, to determine what actually happened and why such burns are possible in the Explorer.
Being a preliminary evaluation, PE26008 should not be confused with a safety recall. The Office of Defects Investigation is understandably investigating right now, specifically the scope, frequency, and safety consequences of the alleged issue. Going forward, the NHTSA could escalate this inquiry.
Through September 2026, the Explorer sold no fewer than 189,210 units in the United States market alone. That's 17.6 percent better compared to the first nine months of 2025, putting the Explorer well ahead of the Bronco Sport and Bronco. Natively rear-wheel drive, the mid-size model is a three-row affair that carries a starting price of $38,680 as of November 2026.
Ford says that combined sales of the Tremor and Platinum increased 59.9 percent, while sales of the lesser Active and ST-Line rose 23.3 percent. Not bad for an aging design. Active is what Ford calls the most affordable specification, which is only available with the 2.3-liter EcoBoost I4.
Tremor customers are presented with either the standard 2.3 or the optional 3.0-liter EcoBoost V6, whereas the ST comes with the 3.0-liter unit by default. Weirdly enough, the luxury-oriented Platinum defaults to the 2.3 instead of the punchier six-cylinder lump.
